title: Connecting Identity Capital and Natural Mentoring
text:
Identity development is shaped by personal experiences, social relationships, and access to opportunities. The Identity Capital Model and natural mentoring offer complementary perspectives on this process. Together, they help explain how relationships may contribute to the resources people develop and use as they navigate college, explore their identities, and consider their futures.connecting
For an overview of each concept, visit the Identity Capital and Natural Mentoring pages.

title: Connecting Identity Capital and Natural Mentoring
section: How Natural Mentoring Connects to Identity Capital
text:
How Natural Mentoring Connects to Identity Capital
Natural mentoring may contribute to identity capital by helping individuals develop resources through their relationships and experiences. These resources can include practical knowledge, skills, professional connections, confidence, and a clearer understanding of personal interests and goals. For example, a student who develops a supportive relationship with a professor may learn about research opportunities, receive guidance on entering the field, and connect with other researchers. These experiences can build practical skills and professional connections while helping the student evaluate whether research aligns with their interests and future plans. In this example, natural mentoring helps explain how support and opportunities emerge through relationships, while identity capital provides a framework for understanding the resources the student develops through those experiences.

title: Connecting Identity Capital and Natural Mentoring
section: A Conceptual Model of Natural Mentoring and Identity Capital
text:
A Conceptual Model of Natural Mentoring and Identity Capital
The model in Figure 1 illustrates a proposed connection between natural mentoring and identity capital. Natural mentoring can provide guidance, encouragement, role modeling, and access to opportunities. Through these experiences, individuals may develop knowledge and skills, social connections, confidence, agency, purpose, and self-understanding. Personal agency and social context influence this process. Individuals interpret experiences and decide how to use the resources available to them, while their environments shape access to relationships and opportunities.



Figure 1. A Conceptual Model of How Natural Mentoring Contributes to Identity Capital


The model represents a proposed conceptual synthesis of the two framework models. Further research is needed to determine how natural mentoring directly contributes to identity capital development.

title: Connecting Identity Capital and Natural Mentoring
section: Reflection: Applying These Concepts to Your Development
text:
Reflection: Applying These Concepts to Your Development
Think about a relationship or experience that influenced how you understood yourself or considered your future.

Who has helped you see a strength, interest, or possibility in yourself that you might not have recognized otherwise?
What have you gained through this relationship? Consider knowledge, skills, confidence, a clearer sense of purpose, or connections to people and opportunities.
Has this person introduced you to an opportunity or future path you had not previously considered? How did that influence your thinking?
Was there advice or an opportunity you chose to pursue, adapt, or decline? What influenced your decision?
What resources would help you reach a current or future goal, and what people or experiences might help you develop them?
Reflecting on these questions can help you recognize how relationships and experiences have contributed to your development and identify resources that may help you move forward.

title: The Relationships That Shape Us: An Informational Resource on Natual Mentoring and Identity Capital in Higher Education
text:
College is more than an academic experience. As students navigate new environments, develop greater independence, explore their values and goals, and make decisions about their futures, these experiences can shape how students understand themselves, the resources they develop, and the possibilities they envision for their lives.
Relationships with supportive adults play an important role in this process. Natural mentoring relationships develop organically through everyday interactions with people such as faculty members, supervisors, coaches, and other trusted adults. Unlike formal mentoring programs, these relationships are not established through an assigned mentoring arrangement. They can offer students guidance, encouragement, knowledge, and perspectives as they navigate college and consider their futures.
The Relationships That Shape Us explores natural mentoring among college students through the lens of Côté’s identity capital model. This resource examines identity capital as a framework for understanding the personal resources individuals develop and draw upon as they navigate social environments, make decisions, and pursue opportunities. By bringing together research on identity capital and natural mentoring, this website explores how supportive relationships may contribute to students’ development and their ability to navigate higher education.

title: The Relationships That Shape Us: An Informational Resource on Natual Mentoring and Identity Capital in Higher Education
text:
Why These Relationships Matter
Students do not navigate higher education with identical experiences, resources, or opportunities. Access to supportive relationships can vary, as can the knowledge, encouragement, and guidance students receive. Understanding natural mentoring means examining not only the potential benefits of these relationships but also the circumstances that make them more or less accessible.
By considering mentoring through the identity capital model, this resource highlights the relationship between social connections and the personal resources students draw upon as they navigate college and plan for their futures.

title: Identity Capital: Understanding Personal and Social Resources
text: The Identity Capital Model (ICM), developed by sociologist James E. Côté provides a framework for understanding the process of young adults finding their place in an increasingly individualistic, complex, and chaotic post-modern world. The model examines how people develop and use personal and social resources as they construct their identities and navigate the opportunities and constraints of their social environments (Côté, 1996, 1997). Through this perspective, identity development involves both the resources individuals acquire and the ways they use those resources to pursue personally meaningful goals.

title: Identity Capital: Understanding Personal and Social Resources
text:
Defining Identity Capital
Identity capital refers to the resources individuals develop and draw upon as they navigate life transitions. Côté’s (1996, 1997) model emphasizes the interaction between individual agency and the social contexts in which identity development occurs, recognizing that although individuals make decisions about who they want to become, their choices are shaped by the opportunities, expectations, and constraints within their environments. Côté and Levine (2016) further conceptualize identity capital in terms of the personal capacities and social resources that individuals accumulate and use to navigate their lives, including psychological strengths, interpersonal skills, knowledge, experiences, and relationships. These resources can influence how individuals approach decisions, respond to challenges, and pursue educational, professional, and personal goals. Within higher education, identity capital provides a useful framework for understanding how students’ experiences contribute to their developing identities and perceptions of future possibilities. Students enter college with varying levels of familiarity with academic institutions, professional expectations, and available opportunities, and their experiences throughout college can expand these resources through interactions with faculty and peers, the acquisition of new knowledge, and participation in academic and professional activities. Consequently, identity capital highlights how students’ developing identities are shaped by the resources they bring to college, the experiences they encounter, and the social environments that influence their opportunities to acquire and use these resources.

title: Identity Capital: Understanding Personal and Social Resources
text:
Tangible and Intangible Resources
The Identity Capital Model encompasses both tangible and intangible resources that influence the navigation and decision-making dilemmas that were mentioned above (Côté, 1997; Côté & Levine, 2016). Tangible resources relate to the qualifications, experiences, and connections individuals can draw upon, whereas intangible resources involve the psychological capacities that support personal agency, self-understanding, and decision-making. Although these categories represent different aspects of identity capital, they work together to influence how individuals pursue opportunities and navigate identity development.

Tangible Resources
Tangible identity capital encompasses resources that individuals can use to access opportunities, navigate social environments, and demonstrate their qualifications or experience. In higher education, these resources may include:

Education and credentials: Degrees, certifications, and other qualifications that demonstrate acquired knowledge or experience.

Social and professional connections: Relationships that provide access to information, guidance, mentorship, and opportunities.

Knowledge and experience: Familiarity with academic expectations, professional environments, and the processes involved in pursuing educational or career goals.

Communication and interpersonal skills: Abilities that support collaboration, relationship development, and effective communication across social settings.

These resources can shape students’ experiences by influencing the opportunities available to them and their ability to recognize and pursue those opportunities. For example, a student who develops a relationship with a professor may learn about an undergraduate research position, gain practical experience working with a research team, and establish additional professional connections. The initial relationship can provide access to an opportunity, while the resulting experience may expand the student’s knowledge, skills, and professional network. This example illustrates how resources can accumulate and create further opportunities over time. However, the value of tangible resources depends partly on the social environments in which individuals use them. A credential, skill, or professional connection may be more useful in some settings than others, depending on the expectations and opportunities within those environments. Identity capital therefore involves more than the resources individuals possess; it also concerns how those resources interact with the social contexts in which identity development takes place (Côté & Levine, 2016).


Intangible Resources
Whereas tangible resources can provide access to opportunities or demonstrate qualifications, intangible identity capital encompasses psychological capacities that support individuals in making decisions, pursuing goals, and navigating their environments. Côté’s work draws attention to personal resources associated with agency and identity development, including self-esteem, a sense of purpose, an internal locus of control, and capacities for reflection and decision-making (Côté, 1996, 1997; Côté & Levine, 2016). In the context of higher education, these resources may be reflected in:

Self-confidence: Confidence in one’s abilities and capacity to pursue goals.

Sense of purpose: An understanding of personal priorities and the goals that provide direction.

Agency: A perceived capacity to make decisions and take action within existing circumstances.

Critical thinking: The ability to evaluate information, consider alternatives, and make informed decisions.

Self-understanding: An awareness of personal experiences, values, interests, strengths, and developing identity.

Intangible resources can influence how students interpret their experiences and respond to opportunities. For example, a student may have access to an undergraduate research position but feel uncertain about their qualifications or ability to succeed. Confidence in their capacity to learn, a clearer understanding of their academic interests, and a willingness to seek guidance may help them pursue the position despite that uncertainty. In this way, psychological resources can influence whether students act on opportunities available to them and how they use the experiences that follow.
Tangible and intangible resources are therefore best understood as interconnected aspects of identity capital. Psychological capacities can influence how individuals seek out relationships, develop skills, and pursue opportunities, while educational experiences and social interactions can strengthen their knowledge, confidence, and sense of direction. Examining both types of resources provides a broader understanding of how students develop the capacities and experiences they draw upon as they navigate higher education and form identities connected to their academic, professional, and personal futures (Côté, 1997; Côté & Levine, 2016).

title: Identity Capital: Understanding Personal and Social Resources
section: How Identity Capital Develops in College
text:
How Identity Capital Develops in College
Identity capital develops over time as individuals draw upon existing resources, engage with new experiences, and acquire additional knowledge, skills, relationships, and personal capacities. Côté’s (1997) research on university students examined identity capital resources and their relationship with subsequent resource acquisition, providing a basis for considering how resources may develop during the transition into higher education. College provides opportunities for this development both inside and outside the classroom. Academic projects, employment, volunteering, campus involvement, personal relationships, and other life experiences can contribute to students’ knowledge, practical skills, social connections, and self-understanding. For example, participating in a research lab may help a student develop technical skills, collaborate with others, and explore whether research aligns with their future goals. The experience may also expand their professional connections and strengthen their confidence in navigating unfamiliar academic environments.
Every student enters college with different experiences and resources, and their development does not follow a single path. Recognizing how resources accumulate over time helps explain how experiences across multiple areas of life can contribute to students’ developing identities and future possibilities.

title: Identity Capital: Understanding Personal and Social Resources
section: Social Context and Access to Resources
text:
Social Context and Access to Resources
Although individuals develop and use identity capital through their experiences and decisions, their opportunities to acquire resources are shaped by their social environments. Family responsibilities, financial circumstances, institutional practices, and access to information and social networks can influence how easily students navigate higher education. Bourdieu’s (1986) work on social and cultural capital highlights how access to valued knowledge, relationships, and institutional opportunities is unevenly distributed. For example, one student may enter college already familiar with undergraduate research opportunities, while another may need to learn how to find positions and approach faculty members. Differences in access to information can influence how students recognize and pursue opportunities, even when they share similar interests and abilities. It is equally important to recognize that students bring resources from experiences beyond formal education. Employment, caregiving, community involvement, and personal responsibilities can contribute practical knowledge, interpersonal skills, and problem-solving abilities. Identity capital provides a way to recognize these existing resources while considering how social environments shape opportunities for further development.

title: Identity Capital: Understanding Personal and Social Resources
text:
Recognizing Your Identity Capital
Reflecting on identity capital involves identifying the resources you have developed, understanding how your experiences have shaped them, and considering how they might support your future goals.
Consider the following questions: 1. What skills, experiences, or relationships have helped you navigate an important transition?
2. What personal strengths have you developed through challenges or unfamiliar experiences?
3. What resources could help you pursue a goal that matters to you?
4. What opportunities would you like to explore, and what might help you access them?

title: Natural Mentoring: The Role of Relationships in Development
text:
Relationships shape how people understand themselves, navigate unfamiliar environments, and consider their futures, as illustrated through the Identity Capital Model. During college, students interact with professors, supervisors, peers, family members, and others who may offer guidance as they pursue academic, personal, and professional goals. Some of these relationships become important capital resources that help students recognize their strengths, explore opportunities, and navigate challenges.
Natural mentoring provides a framework for understanding how meaningful mentoring relationships can emerge through everyday social interactions. Rather than requiring a formal mentoring program, these relationships develop through existing social networks and communities, allowing guidance and support to emerge as individuals’ needs and circumstances change.

title: Natural Mentoring: The Role of Relationships in Development
text:
Defining Natural Mentoring
Natural mentoring refers to supportive relationships that develop organically through existing social networks and communities (Zimmerman et al., 2005). These relationships may form between students and professors, employees and supervisors, students at different stages of development, or individuals and members of their families and communities. Natural mentors are commonly defined as an older, more experienced adult who takes an interest in another person’s development and provides support through their relationship. Following Hurd et al. (2016), natural mentors are distinguished from parents or other parental figures, friends, and romantic partners. Other relatives, such as grandparents, aunts, uncles, or cousins, may qualify as natural mentors if they provide guidance and support outside a parental role. Natural mentors may be people students knew before college or adults they meet during their college experience. This support may include encouragement, sharing knowledge and experiences, offering guidance, serving as a role model, or connecting someone with new opportunities. Over time, continued interaction and mutual trust can allow these relationships to become meaningful sources of developmental support.

title: Natural Mentoring: The Role of Relationships in Development
text:
How Natural Mentoring Supports Development
Natural mentoring relationships can support development in several interconnected ways. Rhodes’s (2005) model of youth mentoring identifies social-emotional, cognitive, and identity development as pathways through which mentoring relationships may influence young people. Although this model focuses on youth mentoring, it offers a useful framework for understanding forms of support that may also be relevant during college.

Emotional and Social Support
Natural mentors can provide encouragement, listen to concerns, and help individuals navigate uncertainty. Supportive relationships create opportunities to discuss challenges, consider different perspectives, and receive constructive feedback. For college students, this support may be particularly valuable when adjusting to unfamiliar academic environments or making decisions about the future. A professor who responds thoughtfully to a student’s concerns, for example, may help the student feel more comfortable asking questions and seeking assistance. Research on youth mentoring programs has identified benefits across behavioral, social, emotional, and academic outcomes, although findings vary according to program and relationship characteristics (DuBois et al., 2011). These findings underscore the importance of relationship quality without establishing that every natural mentoring relationship produces the same outcomes.


Knowledge and Guidance
Mentors can help individuals understand expectations, navigate unfamiliar environments, and identify practical steps toward their goals. In higher education, this guidance may involve finding research opportunities, preparing for graduate school, developing professional skills, or learning how to access university resources. Relationships can also provide access to information and resources that individuals may not possess independently. Bourdieu’s (1986) work on social capital helps explain how social connections can facilitate access to resources, while Hagler’s (2018) network-based mentoring model examines how naturally occurring relationships with institutional agents can help students navigate educational environments. These perspectives highlight the value of having someone who can explain not only which opportunities exist, but also how to pursue them.


Role Modeling and Identity Development
Natural mentors can influence how individuals understand their abilities and envision their futures. Observing another person’s experiences, decisions, and responses to challenges can introduce possibilities that individuals may not have previously considered. Rhodes (2005)identifies role modeling as one pathway through which mentoring relationships may contribute to identity development, while Hagler (2018) considers the role of natural mentoring in students’ development within educational settings. For example, a student unfamiliar with academic research may benefit from a professor who shares their career experiences and explains the range of opportunities available in psychology. This interaction may help the student consider research as a possible career path and evaluate whether it aligns with their interests. Markus and Nurius’s (1986) concept of possible selves provides a complementary perspective, emphasizing how people’s ideas about who they might become relate to their self-concept and motivation. Mentors may contribute to this process by encouraging exploration and helping students recognize possibilities they had not previously considered.

title: Natural Mentoring: The Role of Relationships in Development
section: Natural Mentoring Before and During College
text:
Natural Mentoring Before and During College
Natural mentoring relationships can support students before they enter college and continue to develop as they navigate higher education. Before college, teachers, coaches, supervisors, and community members may help students explore their interests, learn about educational opportunities, and prepare for unfamiliar expectations. These relationships can provide guidance as students make decisions about their futures and begin navigating the transition to higher education. For example, a high school teacher who encourages a student’s academic interests may help them recognize their strengths and consider opportunities they had not previously imagined. A coach or community mentor may share practical advice about pursuing educational goals or connecting with people who have relevant experience. Such relationships may help students develop knowledge, confidence, and connections they can draw upon when entering college.
Natural mentoring opportunities also emerge during college. Professors, supervisors, graduate students, peers, and community members may help students understand academic expectations, explore career paths, and access new opportunities. Some relationships develop through repeated interaction in classrooms, research laboratories, campus employment, and student organizations. Others emerge through less-frequent interactions that introduce students to new information or social networks. Students enter college with different experiences, support systems, and access to opportunities. Some may already have supportive mentors, while others may develop meaningful relationships after arriving on campus. Recognizing the value of both existing relationships and new connections helps students consider where they can find guidance, learn from others’ experiences, and expand their opportunities for development.

title: Natural Mentoring: The Role of Relationships in Development
text:
Recognizing Natural Mentoring Relationships
Natural mentoring relationships can be difficult to recognize because they often develop through ordinary interactions rather than formal arrangements. Someone who consistently offers thoughtful feedback, shares relevant experiences, encourages your development, or helps you explore opportunities may be serving as a natural mentor even if neither person uses that term. Reflecting on your existing relationships can help you recognize the different forms of support available to you and identify areas where additional guidance might be useful.
Consider the following questions:

Who has helped you navigate an important decision or unfamiliar situation?

Who has shared knowledge or experiences that helped you understand an academic, professional, or social environment?

Which relationships have encouraged you to explore interests or opportunities you had not previously considered?

What kinds of support would be helpful as you work toward your current goals?

Where might you find opportunities to connect with people who have relevant experiences or share your interests?


Natural mentoring highlights the developmental importance of relationships that emerge through everyday life. Recognizing these connections can help individuals better understand their sources of support and the ways relationships contribute to their ongoing personal, academic, and professional development.
